title: Partners in Workforce Development
author: Morgen Peers
body:
The gap, in the City's own words

The Bayfront Industrial Area Strategy, approved by Council in September 2022, lists 47 actions. Action 42 is short-term:

    "Form partnerships with local institutions to create space for start-up research and innovation opportunities working towards creation of a physical and digital campus. These partnerships will also work towards bridging education and employee training programs with businesses in the area."

The 2024 Action Plan Update (PED14117(e)) records where it stands: of 47 actions, 6 achieved, 13 initiated, 28 not started. Progress tracking was paused in early 2024. The theme "Creating an Advanced Manufacturing & Innovation Campus" sits at 0 achieved, 1 initiated, 5 not started, and the initiated item is pedestrian and cycling amenities.

To be precise about our claim: Paton Hall sits in Strathcona, outside the Bayfront study area, and has no standing in that strategy. We are pointing out that the City identified a function, called it short-term, and has not started it — and that we perform that function now, at no municipal cost.

What we are

One open room of roughly 2,000 sq ft in a garage that has been in mechanical use since about 1927. Concrete floor, garage height, a bay door large enough to drive a machine through, parking on site.

The people are the ones your intake misses: the millwright with an idea, the controls engineer between jobs, the founder with a working prototype and no company yet. They are building hardware, robotics, software and industrial products, and they are not enrolling or applying anywhere.

The model is membership-funded and volunteer-operated. Fifty-one members covers the entire operating cost. There is no funding gap to close before we can be useful to you.

What we want from you

Not money, in the first instance.

    Recognition of training quality — a partner who can vouch for what is taught here, so seminars carry weight beyond our own say-so.
    Referrals — the people who approach you and do not fit.
    Speakers and instructors — your people, in a room full of ours.
    A named contact who will take a call.

Certified training

We are in conversation with EPTAC about hosting certified IPC training in Hamilton — electronics inspection and standards to begin with, the credential the industry actually checks for. Nothing is signed and we will not describe it as more than that.

The context that matters to you: the Ontario Job Grant (relaunched May 2026, up to $10,000 per trainee) and Skills Development Fund Round 5 ($150M, opened June 2026) mean regional employers can often have this training funded. The demand exists and the money exists. The delivery point is what is missing.

The terms of engagement

The lease at our preferred site is one year, on a building that carries a redevelopment proposal — which is why the rent works. Everything we own comes apart and travels, and other Hamilton properties are being actively scouted.

We say that at the start rather than let you find it later. What we are asking you to back is a membership and a method, not an address

title: Call to Participate
author: Morgen Peers
body:
There is a room at 4 Breadalbane Street in Hamilton that has been a mechanics shop since about 1927, and we are not going to change it. One open room. Concrete floor, garage height, a bay door you can drive a vehicle through. Benches and stools along one wall for hardware, prototyping and testing; blackboards and whiteboards along the other. A pool table at the back with a cap that drops over it when the table is needed for something larger than a game. That is the whole building, and it is deliberately the whole plan. What happens in it depends entirely on who decides to show up. 

The idea is not new, and we are not pretending it is. Around 1800, George Birkbeck started giving scientific instruction to working mechanics in Glasgow. By 1823 that had become the Glasgow Mechanics' Institution, and the model spread quickly enough that the Hamilton and Gore Mechanics' Institute was founded here in 1839, operating at first out of rented rooms. The premise then was that people who work with their hands are entitled to the theory behind the work, that the instruction is best delivered by peers rather than sold down from a height, and that a shared room with tools and a library beats ten people each struggling alone. None of that has been disproved. It has mostly just been forgotten in places that used to know it well. 

Hamilton is a strange and good place to remember it. This is still a working industrial city — a port that moves steel and ore and grain, rail yards, mills that have outlasted every prediction of their closing. The industrial capacity is real and it is still here. What has thinned out is the connective tissue: the places where somebody who fixes machines for a living can learn microcontrollers, where somebody who writes software can put their hands on a bench and find out what it costs to make a physical thing, where a person with a product idea can meet the three people who know how to build it. Those people all live here already. They mostly do not have a room in common. 

So the room is the offer, and the specifics are ordinary on purpose: work tables and fixed benches, assembly zones for projects that need to stay standing between sessions, a tool room, storage bins so a project does not have to travel home with you, and boards meant to be written on and left up. Alongside that, training with certifications that carry weight on a résumé — IPC and J-STD electronics standards, Linux systems, microcontrollers — taught in partnership with certified instructors rather than improvised. Anyone can rent the space or the room for an event. Members get the rest, and members set the direction. 

It is not open yet. The corporation is forming, the building is identified, the first courses and partnerships are getting lined up, and the membership is being raised now, before the doors open, because that is what determines whether they open at all. This is not a finished institution looking for customers; it is a founding cohort deciding what a hardware hall in this city should be, at the stage where those decisions are still genuinely open. Some of what is written on this site will turn out to be wrong, and the people who join early are the ones who will articulate the direction of the hub. 

If any of that sounds like your kind of problem, there are several honest ways in. Join the mailing list and watch — that costs nothing and commits you to nothing. Commit to a membership at Bench, Shop or Keyholder and start using the room from the day it opens. Payment for one month or electively for the 1st year will be collected before the lease is signed. Take a Founder membership if you want your name permanently attached to the group that made it possible. If you run a business that depends on skilled technical people in this region, the Patron and Champion tiers exist so you can sponsor equipment, a workshop series, or a zone, and have that recognised. And if you would like to teach something, or want a course that is not yet on the calendar, tell us — the training schedule is built from what members actually ask for. Write to patonhall.canada@gmail.com. The room is here. It's been here since 1927. The only open question is who is going to be in it now. You?
